maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I understand the minister has recently been attending meetings of the advisory committee to the United Nations emergency force in New York. Has there been any change in Nasser's stand that all tolls must be paid to Egypt by shipping passing through the Suez canal?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: No, I do not know of any change in the position of the Egyptian government from that laid out in their memorandum of arrangements for the canal which was made public by them last week.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question supplementary to the one I asked him earlier this morning. Press dispatches indicate that Washington has issued a cautionary notice for United States ships to avoid using the Suez canal. Can the minister give the house any information concerning this move and let us know whether Canada is taking a similar course, or contemplating any such course with regard to Canadian ships?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no information to substantiate the statement made by my hon. friend, but we have been in touch in the last few days with the United States and with certain other governments with regard to a declaration made by the Egyptian government, and circulated to one or two of the main users of the canal, covering the arrangements which the government of Egypt proposes for the use of the canal when it is open to shipping. As I say, we are discussing that memorandum with the United States government. In so far as any precautionary actions relating to Canadian ships are concerned, that matter will be considered when we have concluded our discussions with the United States and other governments. But, as I understand it, there were only two or three Canadian ships which used the canal last year. So it is not a matter of immediate urgency so far as Canadian shipping is concerned.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Can the minister get further information concerning this United States move and advise the house, perhaps tomorrow?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext:
Well, I will be glad to find out. As a matter of fact, as I have said, Mr. Speaker, we are in touch with the United

States government to ascertain, if possible, what action it proposes to take in the light of this Egyptian document.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: A further question: Has Nasser notified the United Nations whether or not he will permit Israeli ships to use the Suez canal? Has he agreed to that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, our position, as one member of the United Nations, in regard to the use of the Suez canal by the ships of all states without discrimination, has been made abundantly clear to the United Nations on more than one occasion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: I asked whether or not Nasser had now agreed to permit the use of the Suez canal to Israeli ships, and I deserve a better answer than the evasive one just given. I am asking for an answer to that question.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the policy of the Egyptian government in respect of the use of the Suez canal has been outlined in a memorandum which was made public by the Egyptian government last week. Perhaps my hon. friend has read that memorandum. If he has, it answers his question.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: It does not say anything about Israel.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: You are very evasive.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I think we should thank the official opposition for the reduction of honest questions.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: That is a great contribution.

maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Following up the question of the Leader of the Opposition, is it not a fact that the statement by Egypt, to which the minister refers, did not deal with the question whether Israel would be permitted to use the canal? The question of Israel's right to use the canal is something else again. Can the minister tell us what position Nasser is taking with regard to the use of the canal by Israeli shipping?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUEZ CANAL-IMPOSITION OF TOLLS BY EGYPT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the document to which I have referred the Egyptian government indicated the arrangements which, in their view, should be instituted for the use of the canal. No reference was made in that document one way or the other to Israeli ships but merely to ships using the canal. We have no information as to what action the Egyptian government will take in regard to Israeli ships using the canal.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct
a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of a news report in the latest issue of the Financial Post to the effect that "more than one-half of Canada's export trade with the United Kingdom and Europe is at stake on decisions to be made by a committee of European experts now meeting in Paris to plan the European free trade area." It is pointed out that Canadian firms exporting either raw materials or semi-processed goods may find themselves in the position within that free trade area where 82715-178J
Inquiries of the Ministry the amount of imported component parts may be reduced in order to qualify for participation within that area. Would the minister say whether or not this matter was discussed with the Prime Minister of Great Britain and what are the hopes that in the achievement of this free trade area Canada's exports, to the degree I have mentioned, will not be in danger of being diminished, if not altogether obliterated?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED EFFECT ON CANADA OF PROPOSED EUROPEAN TRADE AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not
seen the article in question but from the description of it given by my hon. friend I would say that the writer has been having nightmares. About 90 per cent of the trade with the United Kingdom and with the free trade area is in the form of metals, foodstuffs and other raw materials. Whatever happens within the area, the demand for these products is not going to be diminished and in my opinion our market for them is not going to be diminished. If there is any barrier put up it will be a barrier against the world and not solely against Canada.
With respect to the 10 per cent of manufactured goods that we sell in that area, we are watching the situation closely. I believe that on balance we do not stand to lose a great deal of trade, whatever happens. The matter was discussed at Bermuda. The United Kingdom shares our apprehensions even though we both realize the benefits that might accrue from the establishment of a free trade area of that kind. We are both watching the situation closely. It will be some months before any country decides to join the agreement. In the meantime discussions will be held, and we hope that the ultimate result will not be damaging to Canada's trade.

He said: The amounts provided by this bill are intended to provide for necessary requirements of the public service during April. The form of the bill is the same as that of similar bills passed in previous years. The passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize any item in the estimates when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply, and the usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.

I want to raise on this supply motion what I do consider to be a genuine grievance, a grievance shared not only by myself but by this parliament and I think the people of Canada. I refer, of course, to the recent incident in which the Prime Minister has admitted he wrote a letter or letters to Mr. Dunton protesting the use by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of a certain gentleman as commentator on the C.B.C. The Prime Minister says he had taken this action as a private citizen and he claimed that that was his right. I have just received a copy of yesterday's Hansard which shows the Prime Minister's remarks

Interim, Supply
and I find where the Prime Minister said that he did have correspondence with Mr. Dunton in October. I omit a line or two at page 2769 and then read where he says:
. . . but as a Canadian citizen, about the tone of a broadcast I had heard.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked:
Would the Prime Minister be willing to table that letter?
The Prime Minister replied:
No, I would not, sir. I would have no objection to showing my hon. friend the correspondence but I would not like to set a precedent that correspondence between a member of the government and someone who happens to be in any one of these crown agencies should be tabled.
I take it, sir, that the leopard has changed his spots and the Prime Minister is now a member of the government writing to one of these crown agencies and has ceased to be the private citizen in which capacity he had protested to the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C.
When I attempted to move the motion for the adjournment of the house this morning I did it with a knowledge that at least I was being consistent. During my years in this house and in the C.B.C. committee I think my colleagues can bear witness to the fact that I have always maintained there should be the greatest amount of freedom in the expression of opinion. That freedom of expression should not be denied to the system of communication which is controlled under the jurisdiction of this parliament, and that it is so controlled is the greater reason in fact why that expression should be free provided all sides of the opinion be given an opportunity of presentation.
My holding these opinions in regard to intellectual freedom has sometimes earned the ire of some hon. members in this house and I think perhaps particularly of some of my friends to my left, the members of the Social Credit party, who have attempted by every perfectly legitimate means at their disposal both in the house and in the committee to keep certain people off the air. Their actions in that regard have always been violently opposed by myself for reasons which I have stated from time to time when the occasion arose.
The fact that the Prime Minister is the Prime Minister is one of the reasons and the greatest reason why he should not have made that attempt. He claims as his right as a private citizen to be critical of the C.B.C. and I admit he is in a very difficult position, but I suggest there are other means he could have taken than to sign a letter. After all, he cannot avoid the fact and

he would not want to that he is the Prime Minister of Canada, but surely he is not sufficiently naive to believe that he can write a letter to the chairman of a crown agency and not add to the opinion that he expresses in such a letter the weight, prestige and influence of the first minister of Canada.
I do not even know the name of this person whom the Prime Minister does not like to hear on the air and thinks it is a waste of public money to have on the air, and I am glad I do not because then I cannot be accused of any ulterior motive in stating this grievance. I do not know the opinion this gentleman put forward nor do I know for what reason the Prime Minister objected to it and I submit that my knowledge of those things would not be relevant to the motion which I attempted to move this morning; but that I do not know these things is the responsibility of the Prime Minister, and the fact that hon. members of this house do not know them is his responsibility since he has refused to table the letters.
As I said a moment ago his reason for that refusal was that he would be creating a precedent. I would say that if the Prime Minister were to go unchallenged for his recent action it would create a precedent which the present Prime Minister and no future prime minister can be allowed to follow. I have asserted vehemently and I assert again that speech must be free and by the same token listening must be free. If we are to restrict freedom of listening we are indulging in the very same practices which we criticize as totalitarian as practised in certain other lands by other peoples.
Certainly there are the rules defined by decency, there are rules in regard to sedition and there is also the protection of the Criminal Code; but the ultimate responsibility for the choice of programs lies with the board of governors of the C.B.C. set up by and responsible to this parliament. To come to an end of the matter quite briefly, sir, because I think I have made my point, it is for parliament to see to it that that body under its jurisdiction must be free to make its own decisions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I join with my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon in protesting most strongly against the action of the Prime Minister last October in writing as he did to the chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I must say at the outset that I was taken by surprise when the Prime Minister made the statement which he gave to the house yesterday. As hon. members will know, I raised this question in the house last Monday

by making reference to Arthur Blakely's column in Monday morning's Montreal Gazette. Hon. members will recall the brevity of the question which I put to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It was brief because I did not think Arthur Blakely's charge was correct. I thought it was a serious charge but I thought the government would surely be in a position to give the lie to it. Accordingly when the Prime Minister stood up yesterday and admitted that as a Canadian citizen or as a member of the government-whichever he wants to choose-he wrote a letter complaining about certain talks that had been given over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I was dumbfounded.
My sense of surprise is all the greater because I recall an exchange that took place in this house a little over a year ago. I refer to an exchange between my friends to my right, my Progressive Conservative friends, and the Minister of National Revenue and the Prime Minister on March 14, 1956.
On that occasion there had been reference to a certain telecast which some hon. members thought not in the best of taste. The hon. member for Eglinton had asked the opinion of the government on this telecast. The Minister of National Revenue-quite rightly I thought at the time and I still think it-refused to state his own opinion on that telecast. Instead he gave an answer which he obtained from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
This was done prior to March 14 and accordingly on that date last year the hon. member for Eglinton rose on a question of privilege and complained that the answer given to his question was an answer supplied by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and that the Minister of National Revenue had not answered my hon. friend's question as to what he himself thought of the particular program.
I remember the incident very well. In fact, I am surprised at my Tory friends getting into this question now as they did yesterday because a year ago they wanted expressions on C.B.C. programming to be given by members of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Characteristically inconsistent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Minister of National Health and Welfare says it is characteristic of the Tories.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I said characteristically inconsistent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister's words are on the record. My contention is that the government is being equally inconsistent, in that it

has departed from the sound position that was taken a year ago by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). On that occasion the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) did not get very far when he sought to raise the matter as one of privilege at the opening of the house on March 14, 1956. He was invited by the Speaker to leave the matter to be dealt with on orders of the day. Accordingly on the orders of the day the hon. member for Eglinton pressed his point and urged the Minister of National Revenue to give his opinion. The minister replied in part as follows, as reported on page 2127 of Hansard:
Now, I am not in charge of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have never interfered in its operations or in its policies. The Department of National Revenue has nothing to do with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The order in council, by which I was appointed, appointed me as the one who would report to parliament for the C.B.C. That I have attempted to do. I purposely have seen that the answers are put as they are, that the C.B.C. replies to the questions that are asked, and they take the full responsibility.
When the hon. member for Eglinton was not satisfied with the refusal of that particular minister, a proper refusal in my view, to state his own opinion on that particular case, he put a question to the Prime Minister in these words:

May I ask the Prime Minister
whether he approves of this type of television broadcast of an actual marriage solemnized, a film being made of it and broadcast on television, at some expense, which he will find set forth on page 2115 of Hansard, including performers' fees?
Here is the reply of the Prime Minister:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has obtained the facts now. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is responsible to parliament. It is a body that has been set up by legislation of parliament, with powers that are provided in that legislation.
I have seen several things on the C.B.C. that I did not think were in good taste. I did not see the telecast to which this question refers, but I have never attempted to exercise any censorship over the activities of the C.B.C. I do not think my personal opinion about the matter in which they select their programs is a matter about which there should be any debate in parliament.
There is no indication in the record as to what happened at that point, but I remember there was applause from this corner of the house at the stand taken by the Prime Minister, that it was not his business any more than it was the business of the Minister of National Revenue to exercise any control or censorship with respect to the programming of the C.B.C.
It is in the light of that proper position which the government took a year ago, even when two ministers were taunted and urged by my friends of the Progressive Conservative party to take an improper position, that it is so strange that only a few months later

Interim Supply
the Prime Minister did what he said he had never done, namely exercise censorship over the activities of the C.B.C.
What censorship?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What censorship? He wrote a letter to the chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation expressing his view that it was not a wise expenditure of public money to put on the air certain talks which he had heard by a certain young professor, who apparently was Professor John Conway of the University of Manitoba at Winnipeg.
Where is the censorship?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Where is the censorship? Apparently there have been no talks since by that same Professor Conway. That is the answer. We do not know yet what that professor said on that occasion. Some reports have reached us as to the nature of the talks, but I hope we will have them in full when they are tabled tomorrow or on Monday by the Minister of National Revenue. Such information as some of us have been able to get would indicate that the talks were not extreme one way or the other. But as the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has said, that does not matter. Surely what is at stake here is the principle of freedom of speech, the principle of the independence of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in its programming from interference by the Canadian government or any member of that government, including the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the Prime Minister tried to say that he has a dual personality, that on the one hand he is a private Canadian citizen who happens to live at 24 Sussex street, Ottawa, and on the other hand he is the Prime Minister of Canada, as he says, through no fault of his own. I think we all know that the Prime Minister cannot have it that way. He knows that he cannot make any utterance that does not carry with it the weight of the Prime Minister of Canada.
Not so very long ago I was endeavouring to have certain papers tabled in the House of Commons which were not tabled and in the course of the discussion the Speaker said that this was a matter which would have to be determined by the government. At that point these words appear on page 2153 of Hansard of March 13, 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I have stated my position on the subject, and I take it that I have stated the position of the government.
That is what the minister said at that particular time. The government did not have to hold a cabinet meeting; the minister did not have to consult with his colleagues. The minister's statement, in view of the

principle of the solidarity of the cabinet, constituted a statement of the position of the government.
A few days ago, on March 26, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) asked a question of one minister of the cabinet. He did not get what to him was a satisfactory reply so he asked another minister. The Speaker interrupted as follows, and I quote from page 2687 of Hansard of that day:
I listened to all questions asked and answers given and when one minister gives government policy, because of government solidarity, that is the answer of the whole cabinet.
I suggest that, when a member of the government, to use the Prime Minister's own words yesterday, writes a letter to the chairman of the board of governors of an emanation of the crown, that is a clear case of government interference with a corporation which should have independence in its programming, that is a clear case of violating the excellent principle which was stated a year ago by both the Minister of National Revenue and the Prime Minister.
On Monday when I put the initial question on this matter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his capacity that day as acting Prime Minister I had assumed that the charge was inflated, that there really was nothing to it. But now that we have had this admission from the Prime Minister that Arthur Blakely was right in the charges he made in his column last Monday, I submit it is time we found out how many such letters have been written to Mr. Dunton by other members of the cabinet. If others have not written letters, I think it is time we knew whether or not there have been phone calls or conversations or suggestions by members of the government that certain people should not be kept on the air.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) might tell us whether he has had any experiences with this sort of thing in days gone by. He might tell us whether there was ever an occassion when his broadcasting was limited. He might tell us whether or not in those days when he was not in the party to which he now belongs any complaint was made that his broadcasting was a little too far to the left, was a little too radical. He could be very helpful in telling us what his experience was at that time. Since he is now in the party perhaps he could find out who it was that complained.
I complained, for one.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) would like to know whether the complaint of my hon. friend from Macleod was sufficient to

get him off the air, or whether there were complaints from Liberals and, particularly, from members of the cabinet.
Mr. Chairman, everyone in the house knows that we in this party have supported the C.B.C. across the years, and that we have supported the government in its defence of public control of radio, and in its policy toward the C.B.C. In fact there were times when we have given stronger support to the government in these matters than have the back benches of the government party, and that is now being acknowledged. We still take that position, and our concern now is not that the C.B.C. has done anything that weakens our faith in that corporation and in the policy of public control of radio. Our concern is with what the Prime Minister has done by writing a letter which because he wrote it was written by the Prime Minister of Canada.
I think a special tribute should go to those who direct the C.B.C. Apparently-and this is one of the reasons we would like to see that correspondence-there was a reply to the Prime Minister by Mr. Dunton in which he set out the position of the C.B.C. and its right to carry on its own programming. It seems to us that if we have freedom of discussion on the C.B.C. in this country it is due to belief in that principle by Mr. Dunton and those around him rather than to sufficient belief in that principle on the part of the government, and Mr. Dunton and his colleagues deserve the tribute of parliament for being sensitive to their responsibility to parliament as a whole rather than any alleged responsibility to the Prime Minister or to the government.
Mr. Chairman, I waited for a moment after my colleague from Saskatoon had sat down, to see whether the Prime Minister had something to say. I hope he will not let this debate go much further without having some statement to make on this matter. If he has any defence, let us hear it. As far as we can see there is no excuse for the Prime Minister interfering in the programming of the C.B.C. in the way he has done.

I, too, am waiting to hear from the Prime Minister what he has to say in this matter. He has not indicated that he is rising at this time, so I will take this opportunity to express a few opinions.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the house experienced a severe shock yesterday when the Prime Minister made the disclosure he did as to the letter he had written to the chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that it was disturbed also by the terms in 82715-179
Interim Supply
which the Prime Minister made that disclosure. The house is aware of the fact that the Prime Minister was not taken by surprise by a question on this matter. The disclosure was not made as the result of any slip of the tongue on the part of the Prime Minister. On the contrary, he had several days' notice, the question having been raised in this house on Monday. So, we may approach the Prime Minister's statement as one made by him deliberately.
Now, sir, the nature of the Prime Minister's statement was, I think, a shock to the house because of the professions that the government has made in times past on the subject of its relations with the C.B.C. and, particularly, because of things which the Prime Minister himself has said on that subject. We have heard, not once but many times, not only the profession but the boast on the part of the government that there is no attempt whatever by it to interfere in any way with the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and never has the government attempted to make any exception in that regard with reference to the programming activities of the corporation.
The attitude which the government has professed in this house has been that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is responsible to parliament, and to parliament alone-not to the government.
The Minister of National Revenue has declared in this house many a time, and has declared in the committee on radio broadcasting many a time, that he is not the minister to whom the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is in any sense responsible, but that he is simply a sort of mouthpiece in the house, or an avenue of communication between the corporation on the one hand and the House of Commons on' the other.
Now, sir, it is well to bear in mind after the tabling yesterday of the report of the Fowler royal commission on the operation of the corporation that the study made by that commission and also the study made by the previous commission, the so-called Massey commission which also considered the operation and set-up of the corporation, alike proceeded on the basis that the corporation is responsible to parliament and to parliament alone. Many of the recommendations of both those royal commissions proceeded on the assumption that there would be a direct responsibility on the part of the corporation to parliament and to parliament alone, and that there would be no relationship between the government and the corporation.
The Prime Minister referred in his statement yesterday to certain broadcasts, but he did not identify them. I do not know

Interim Supply
what those broadcasts were. I certainly have concluded that I did not hear them. It might well be that if I had heard those broadcasts I would have disagreed with the opinions expressed by the broadcasters just as strongly as, evidently, the Prime Minister did. I can only conjecture as to that. It is the right of anyone to disagree with any opinion expressed over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, just as it is the right of any citizen in a free country to disagree with an opinion expressed in any other form.
Had I heard that broadcast, I might have concluded that according to my ideas it was not the kind of use I should like to see made of public funds and that opinions of that nature should not be put over the air at public expense-for public expense is certainly involved. But as to that I can express no certainty. I must simply accept the fact that the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, declared before the committee on broadcasting times without number, is that it seeks to give to the listeners over the years a variety of opinions and, somehow, to achieve what it calls balance in opinion broadcasts.
Canadian opinion.

Not just Canadian opinion. That is a very ill-considered interruption by the hon. member for Kootenay East. A great many of the opinion broadcasts which have been put over the air at public expense are on the part of people who are not in any way Canadians. That is a silly interjection. Evidently the hon. member is not aware of the kind of opinion broadcast which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has sometimes paid substantial amounts of money to give to the Canadian people.
The next striking and shocking thing about the Prime Minister's statement yesterday in this regard is that he stripped away the pretence that the government has maintained, now, for many a year. I am sure I do not need, Mr. Chairman, to expand on the subject of the danger of government interference in the matter of broadcasting of opinions by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Please note, sir, that I said "government interference". I have chosen that expression deliberately.
The danger of government interference is a hundred-fold more serious in a country such as ours in which broadcasting is controlled in all its forms by one government-appointed corporation, and where all the national broadcasting is carried on by that corporation. It is the only medium through which opinion can be broadcast all across Canada. It is a crown corporation, and if that

crown corporation in its programming activities is subject to government interference at any time, then, sir, we shall have created here a weapon in the hands of government which could be used for the purpose not only of throttling expressions of contrary public opinion but for exercising such an' unfair and improper influence on the people as to make government in this country a dangerous leviathan.
Now, sir, so far as we in the official opposition are concerned we will always in this regard stand firmly for two principles of unchallengeable validity. The first is that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation shall be responsible to parliament alone and not to the government and, second, that there shall be on the part of the government no interference whatever with the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in particular with its programming activities and above all its programming activities in relation to opinion broadcasts.
It is quite evident that what the Prime Minister did last fall was in fact to attempt to influence the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with regard to the broadcasting of opinion. No person in this chamber is going to be so naive as to construe what the Prime Minister did, in the light of what he said yesterday, as anything but an attempt to influence the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with reference to opinion broadcasting.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
I am going to be pressed a little for time, but if my hon. friend will wait until I have finished my remarks I will be glad to deal with his question if there is time.
Do you think it is wrong-

a communication was written or would be understood by the receiver as having been written by the right hon. gentleman as a private citizen? How can the Prime Minister of Canada ever be a private citizen as long as he holds that office and is expressing opinions to a crown corporation in relation to a matter of public interest and concerning the expenditure of public money? It was an amazing fiction and I am sure we will never hear anything to equal it in this house as long as any one of us is here.
I wish to say a word in conclusion concerning the attitude of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, particularly of its senior officials and naturally in particular of Mr. Dunton, the chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I have had occasion in the committee on radio broadcasting frequently to bring up questions of C.B.C. policy, C.B.C. administration and C.B.C. broadcasting activities, which have been at variance with the views of Mr. Dunton. We have oftentimes differed quite strongly in the opinions which have been expressed, but I will say this: I have always, in this house and in the committee, defended the right, the untrammelled right, of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to state its position and to take its responsibility. Mr. Dunton has said repeatedly in that committee, "I take responsibility for this; the corporation takes responsibility for it." Not infrequently Mr. Dunton, when these questions have been raised, has admitted that the broadcasting corporation has made a mistake, and that the kind of mistake that was made on occasions referred to would not be repeated on other occasions. On other occasions he has stoutly defended, as is his undoubted right, the programs of the corporation in the face of criticisms expressed by members of the committee.
As long as I am a member of parliament I certainly intend to defend Mr. Dunton's right to support the policies and defend the programming activities of the corporation even when I disagree with them. But when there is disagreement, sir, let it be in the proper place, let it be in the houses of parliament. Parliament is supreme; parliament is the body to which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is responsible. And in this particular if, as appears from the statement made by the Prime Minister yesterday, Mr. Dunton resisted the attempt of the Prime Minister to influence the programming activities of the C.B.C., then I say this parliament owes a debt of gratitude to Mr. Dunton for having stood firmly for a principle that the Prime Minister ought to have been the first to uphold and which at that time he evidently was discarding and repudiating.

Therefore, sir, there is here a clear-cut issue at stake, an issue that does not concern what was said in the broadcast, for I still do not know what was said. I might disagree with the opinions expressed in that broadcast just as strongly as the Prime Minister evidently did. But I do say, sir, that it is a dangerous step that the Prime Minister has taken here. It is a step so dangerous that if this sort of thing should ever set an example either for the Prime Minister himself on future occasions or for any of his ministers, or any ministers in any future government, then, sir, the result of this tampering could have the greatest dangers for public freedom and for the right of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to function without a form of interference which, if it is repeated or pressed, could trammel and could endanger freedom of expression and freedom of thought in Canada.

What I wanted to ask the hon. member for Eglinton was to deal with the questions that he raised in my mind in his speech. He indicated that he, as a leading member of the Progressive Conservative party, and one who I presume would be a member of the government in the future if they were to be elected-

-takes the attitude that he has the right to criticize the C.B.C. in this house because it is responsible to parliament. If he has the full right to do that, I was wondering whether he felt that right did not extend to every other member of parliament, and whether he would say that any member on the government side including a member of the government did not have the same right at least to criticize. Where does he draw the line?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member's question is interesting because it presages events to come. It is quite evident he has exposed what is in his mind in the shape of things to come, and we trust will come very soon.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: "A plague on both your houses."

Mr. Chairman, so far as what the next government will do is concerned, I suggest the hon. member address his question to the man who will be the head of the next government, the Leader of the Opposition.
Oh, oh.

So far as he wishes my opinion as to the relationship between the next government and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation let me say this. Any

Conservative administration would stand firm for the maintenance and the full respect of those two principles I stated today: first, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, created by parliament, shall be responsible to parliament and parliament shall be free. It shall be free to discuss these matters, as it ought. The other principle that would be observed would be that there should be no interference by the government with the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There would be no attempt at that kind of influence which was exerted by this kind of letter, or attempted to be exerted by this kind of letter, and there certainly would not be, in the face of what has been done here, any attempt to turn around and pretend, in the face of the inescapable facts, that a Prime Minister, in relation to a public matter and the expenditure of public moneys by a public crown corporation, can act or speak as a private citizen and not as the head of the government.

speechtext: May I ask a question?
Yes.

-I have passed such letters on to the corporation frequently. Whenever they have come in I have passed them on, and I have often asked-I should not say "often"-I have asked the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on several occasions whether I could see the text of a particular broadcast, and I have used information of that kind, the text of broadcasts, to bring such matters before the committee on radio broadcasting for discussion, as any member ought to do, as any member on such a committee has the right to do.

No, any member of this house has the right.

Any member of this house has the right that I was speaking of to bring these matters before the committee. Of course he has. And if any member of the house wants to do that, if he is not a member of the committee, then certainly he should come before the committee, or he could bring his complaints before the committee through a member of the committee. But, sir, that is a very different thing, a private member of the house doing that, from the Prime Minister of Canada as head of the government doing that very same thing.
Now, we had an example in this house last summer when apparently members of the government, or at least members of the Liberal party, stung by the way in which the public had reacted to their shocking behaviour in the pipeline debate, then sought to make complaints in this house that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in its news broadcasts, was in fact reporting the events of this house in a manner that a Liberal member here argued was reflecting unfavourably upon the government. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
all I can say is that the reply of the hon. member has demonstrated the hypocrisy of the speech he made prior to the question.

The comment that has come from the minister is about what one would expect from one who has frequently sought to ride roughshod over parliament. Any statement in this house of a principle that a crown corporation is responsible to parliament of course would be unacceptable to the minister because he has never had any idea yet of any crown corporation being responsible to anybody but himself. It is for that reason that even though in this way he invades the normal spheres of other departments in the government, he sees to it that half of all the crown corporations are responsible to him. We know just about how difficult it is in those cases for parliament to exercise any attempt at a serious review of the activities of those corporations,

Interim Supply
so it is very difficult for this minister to understand that the relationship between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and parliament is supposed, according to the statements made by the government and according to the statutes, to be a very different kind of relationship from that which exists between parliament on the one hand and any other crown corporation on the other.
This principle has been laid down time and again, and it has been repeated in this house time and again by government spokesmen that this corporation is responsible to parliament alone and not to the government. Therefore, sir, we are going to continue to stand firm for the principle that the corporation is responsible to parliament and that parliament shall be free, according to parliamentary procedures, to exercise its responsibility in the freest sense with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We shall continue to resist, as Liberal members who have any appreciation of what the word "liberal" once meant in this country ought to resist, any attempt on the part of the government to exercise governmental interference over the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and in particular the broadcasts of opinion in relation to public matters.

The hon. member has not
answered the question I put to him, so I shall repeat it. I believe he takes the attitude that it is all right for him to write Mr. Dunton criticizing programs although he is a leading member of the Progressive Conservative party and one who, I am sure, considers himself as a possible minister in a government if that party were to be elected. -Nobody expects that but themselves-but if they do is there any real difference between writing letters to Mr. Dunton criticizing programming actions as a potential member of the government and any other member of parliament on this side of the house even one who is a member of the government writing letters protesting the programming? If the hon. member believes it is right for him to do it does he say it is wrong for anybody on the Liberal side to do it? They are also members of parliament. This board is not sacrosanct; it is responsible to parliament and so to members of parliament. Have we not the same rights as members of the opposition?

I wrote a letter and when asked if I had written any letter I answered that I had written one.
I made no attempt to keep this young man off the air. I did suggest that it might not be too bad if he were introduced and described as the person he is but that I felt it was a misuse of the funds that had to be appropriated by parliament and that we have to recommend to parliament to be appropriated to have that kind of persiflage tone used in a so-called historical description of what had been the policy of Canada as a nation. I did suggest that if I were a member of the opposition I would severely criticize the appropriation of funds for that kind of broadcast.
I felt sure that this was not something that had been chosen by Mr. Dunton and I suggested that there should be someone who had a sense of real responsibility to see to it that matters of that kind were not provided at public expense. I was told that there were only two of these broadcasts. I heard the second broadcast and I had a copy of the first. I think I had a copy of the first one before I wrote

Mr. Chairman, the explanation by the Prime Minister does not clarify the situation at all. It places the Prime

Minister in the position of being a censor for the protection of Canadians from puerile propaganda. That is a most unusual position for the Prime Minister to take. After all, if he believes in freedom of expression an institution of mass propaganda such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should have available to it all degrees of expression. Are we to believe that the Prime Minister has the right to say to the chairman of a board who has a responsibility to parliament that he should not operate according to his ideas of the best interests, but should interfere so that those who take their places as broadcasters and commentators should be introduced by showing the degree of their intelligence, their age, their period in Canada, and their qualifications. This seems to me an example of supercilious censoriousness that is not in keeping with the maintenance of freedom of speech within this country.
After all, what the Prime Minister objects too apparently, is that the foreign policy of this country was represented as being careful about any action of a positive nature. Have we come to the point when commentators must always praise the foreign policy of this government? Are commentators to be chosen on the basis of the degree to which they will praise the government? Surely not. Freedom of speech demands the right of the other person to express his viewpoint, and that is particularly necessary in the preservation of the inviolability of an institution such as the C.B.C.-the right of each individual to express his viewpoint, limited and circumscribed only by the laws of libel and slander, blasphemy and decency. To say that the Prime Minister has the right, or, indeed, that he can defend the right to communicate with the chairman of the C.B.C., with all the vast authority and prestige which the position of Prime Minister carries is one of the most outrageous propositions that have ever been advanced in this house.
It denies freedom of speech. It denies that the C.B.C. may broadcast programs which are not agreeable to the susceptibilities of the Prime Minister. Why did the Prime Minister write the letter? Was it not to prevent such commentators being employed on the C.B.C. in the future? Was not that the purpose? If it was, it was an interference that cannot be justified. It has every appearance of being just that, for the explanation given by the Prime Minister, far from explaining the situation, adds force to the criticism offered here this morning by the hon. member for Eglinton, namely, that this is, indeed, interference with the C.B.C. to a degree that cannot be condoned and which cannot pass unchallenged.

This is not the first time there has been strong suspicion that ministers of the crown have interfered as far as they were able with the C.B.C. and its policies with regard to broadcasting. We remember the case of Bernard Ostry whose offence was that he did not idealize the former prime minister when he wrote a book on that subject, and whether I agree with all the contents of that book or not, Ostry was denied the right to broadcast over the C.B.C. after the programs had been arranged. Why? There can be only one answer-that some member of the government persuaded the C.B.C. that it would not be in the interest of the government of this country that those broadcasts should be made. There could be no other reason. There was no question of blasphemy. There was no question of libel. There was no question of indecency. But there was a very strong possibility that what this man might say would be regarded politically as detrimental to this government.
I say to the Prime Minister, and I do not wish to carry the matter any further, that I hope this will be a lesson to the members of this government that interference, indirectly or directly, direct or subtle, will not be condoned. Interference of this kind can only destroy the independence of the C.B.C. and dry up the wells of information to which the Canadian people are entitled.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that out of this rather sorry business there is only one thing in which we can take comfort, and that is that the Prime Minister has revealed himself as an honest man. I imagine that at this moment some of his colleagues may be feeling he has been embarrassingly honest, in that he has not attempted to hide either what he said on this occasion or the underlying motives that caused him to say what he did.
I was particularly interested in his comment that had it been the Leader of the Opposition who expressed these very decided criticisms of government policy-I think we must accept that that is what it was-I did not hear the broadcasts, but judging from the Prime Minister's description of them they appear to have contained criticism of the government-the Prime Minister told us that had the Leader of the Opposition expressed these views-

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, before we rose for lunch I was pointing out what struck me as a rather extraordinary position the Prime Minister had taken with regard to the propriety of different individuals making the sort of criticism of government policy about which he complained. He indicated that, had it been a member of the House of Commons who had made these criticisms, while he would have regretted it he would not have felt that it was a matter about which he must protest but that because they had been made by a young man, a university professor who had not been long in this country, he considered it highly improper. That appears to me, Mr. Chairman, to reveal a rather curious concept of the freedom of speech in this country, the suggestion that only those whom I described earlier as being politically licensed can come out with statements of this kind.
Since I spoke before lunch I have had the opportunity of reading the scripts of the two addresses and they reveal quite plainly that throughout the addresses criticism was directed not at the Canadian people but at the Canadian government and specifically at the two secretaries of state for external affairs who have had charge of Canada's external relations since 1946. There is only one place where it might be suggested that there was a criticism of the Canadian people, and that is in the final sentence of the second broadcast, the sentence to which the Prime Minister has already referred, the sentence which contained the phrase about Canada not getting its little toes burned. Even that sentence need not necessarily be taken as a criticism of the Canadian people because the question is asked whether the Canadian government will be prepared to ask the Canadian people for support in a less timid policy and it is open to question whether the question is supposed to be asked of the

Interim Supply
Canadian government or to be asked by the Canadian government of the Canadian people.
However, I was struck very much throughout the reading of the whole of these scripts with the fact that the criticisms contained in them were criticisms that have been voiced in this chamber many times during the four years I have been here, and I cannot for the life of me see on what grounds the Prime Minister objects to criticism of his government's policy, criticism of the manner in which Canada has played her part in the world, because surely that is a part of the democratic process.
Nor can I attach very much importance to his suggestion that because this young man has only been in Canada a comparatively short time his opinions therefore should not be listened to. In fact, I rather gathered that the Prime Minister felt it would have been all right if when this young man was introduced he had been introduced as a young man very newly arrived in Canada with no valid views on Canadian policy and not to be taken too seriously, whereas, of course, if the Leader of the Opposition were to voice these views then everyone would know that he was a native son of Canada and an expert on Canada's external relations. Perhaps that should not be taken too seriously too, as one of my colleagues mentions. However, I would suggest to the Prime Minister that very often the outsider has a clearer view of what is taking place than those who are in the midst of the situation.
The Prime Minister's position is, I think, quite peculiar, and it does raise some fundamental questions. During the luncheon recess the question was asked me if the position I was taking implied that there are 19 people in Canada who must not express criticism of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the officials of that corporation. I think the answer to that must really be yes, that they cannot, and the reason that they cannot is very simple because in their hands lies the power to do something about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I would take the same position with regard to a private member of the house who wrote to the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. and suggested to him that unless he altered his programming to suit the member's wishes he would rise in the House of Commons and criticize the corporation. I do so because again he would be using his very much smaller power of attack on the C.B.C.
I suggest to you, sir, that the proper action for the members of the government of Canada in this regard is to bring the matter to parliament and tell us of their objections to the conduct of the C.B.C. and of their plans

for correcting the situation. The Prime Minister did tell us this morning that he thought he had consulted some of his colleagues. I suggest to you that admission means that what the Prime Minister was doing when he wrote his private letter to Mr. Dunton was in effect to tell Mr. Dunton the views of the government, not the views of Mr. St. Laurent, private Canadian citizen. There had been some discussion.
The Prime Minister objected this morning to what he called the historical description of Canada. When I read the script I thought that was perhaps a rather generous and sweeping description of this young man's broadcast. It was hardly a historical description of Canada. It was a recital of the actions of Canadian governments during the last decade, actions which this young man in many instances criticized. With some of his criticisms I agree, with some I do not agree, but the point is that he was exercising what surely must be a right of Canadian citizens.
I would refer the Prime Minister to the recent judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada when two of the justices stressed again and again in the course of their judgment the necessity for complete freedom of discussion in Canada both in parliament and out of parliament if the parliamentary democratic institution is to survive and function properly. In this instance I suggest that it was perfectly legitimate discussion of Canada's governments in the past and perfectly legitimate criticism of those actions, whether or not one agrees with all the points. I wondered when I read the scripts whether perhaps the key to the Prime Minister's rather extraordinary action might be found in the words he used-he will correct me if I am wrong-when he referred to the supercilious tone of the young man in making his remarks on the air.
That may very well be true. I wonder whether the Prime Minister listened to another C.B.C. broadcast not long ago when a very distinguished British author and former diplomat discussed on the radio the difficulties encountered by those like himself who are afflicted with an English accent, the difficulty of being able to convey to his hearers anything but the effect of superciliousness and condescension. That I can readily understand, since I to some extent suffer from the same affliction myself. I can readily understand it may be quite irritating and annoying, but I do not think it is a basis for criticizing the content of a broadcast. In fact, sir, I wonder whether there is not something more profound revealed in this, something more profound in the way of showing us what is the Prime Minister's

conscious or unconscious concept of society. I refer to the distinction he drew between members of this house and other people criticizing government policy. It occurred to me that perhaps unconsciously the Prime Minister has certain traces of authoritarian concept of society; that there are certain people who have privileges of discussion that cannot be accorded to the common herd, and, in particular, cannot be accorded to those who just recently arrived in our midst.
I want to emphasize again, Mr. Chairman, the necessity of our being quite sure, and of the people of Canada being quite sure, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is supported by the people of Canada, is completely free of any domination by the government of the day, or indeed, by the opposition of the day, or, indeed, subject to pressures from private members of this house; because I do not think it can perform its function unless the people are fully convinced of that fact.
I suggest again, sir, that the place for the criticism that the Prime Minister voiced in his letter to Mr. Dunton was the floor of this House of Commons. There are many of us here who deal with the C.B.C. when it comes before the house; there are many who criticize C.B.C. programs. I would say again I think that is part of our right, and part of our duty, but it is not the part of our duty and right to write ahead of time to Mr. Dunton and to warn him and say, "Because I do not like this program I am going to attack you on the floor of the house if you do not change it in the meantime." That effect would really be the effect of the Prime Minister's letter.
I am not going to deal with the Prime Minister's suggestion that he wrote as a private citizen. I really do not think he expected us to take that very seriously, because there are certain things that people forfeit when they achieve certain positions. I suggest to you, sir, that the person who occupies the position of Prime Minister of Canada does, to a very large extent, forfeit his rights and privileges as an ordinary Canadian citizen. He cannot divest himself of his office as easily as all that.
Finally, sir, I would suggest to the Prime Minister that really he is far too fearful of the effects of broadcasting of this sort. I say quite frankly I do not think they were very good broadcasting techniques; I think they were rather poor. I would draw his attention to a distinguished Canadian who occupies the opposite position in London. I imagine that most of us have heard Mr. Robert McKenzie, a distinguished British Columbian, on the British Broadcasting Corporation broadcasts. Mr. McKenzie on

many occasions criticizes not merely the government of Great Britain but the attitude and actions of the British people themselves, and I have heard of no suggestion that the Prime Minister of Great Britain, or any member of the British House of Commons, has sought to bring pressure to bear on the British Broadcasting Corporation to put a stop to Mr. McKenzie's frank talks about the state of affairs in Great Britain.
I want to conclude, sir, by saying what I said at the beginning. I am sure there is one thing that has come out of this. The Prime Minister is an honest man. He told us quite frankly that he had done this. I submit, sir, that he was disastrously mistaken in his judgment and I hope we can be assured that in the future, if he or his colleagues have reason to feel that the C.B.C. in its programs is not behaving in the interests of the Canadian people, they will frankly bring the matter before parliament and tell us what they propose to do to correct the situation, rather than to subject public servants, who have no means whatever of publicly protecting themselves, to pressures of the sort that were exerted by the Prime Minister in this case.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister has had several lectures now on this matter, and it is not my intention to read him another one, but I do want him to think that on a matter as important as this I should say something and express at least an opinion.
There are principles involved which I believe ought to be most carefully scrutinized, and perhaps by saying something I might be able to help to crystallize the views of the house on this important matter. I do not know a thing about what the Prime Minister wrote in his letter except what he has said here. I did not even know a letter was written by him until he admitted it in answer to a question yesterday. I did not hear the broadcast in question; I do not know Professor Conway, and I do not know what his purpose was on the air at all, or who asked him to speak, or what he was supposed to be speaking about. But I do know these important things in connection with the principle.
When the hon. member for Saskatoon was speaking this morning he appeared to imply, if not to say, that some of his colleagues to the left, meaning us, had attempted on occasion to keep someone off the air. If I have misstated his implication I would like to have it set straight.

I said, Mr. Chairman, when they did it on a previous occasion it was in a good, legal and proper manner, and that was on the floor of this house.

Having that position made clear, I do want to say that the position that my colleagues and I have always taken with regard to freedom of expression-and that matter is involved in this whole discussion- is this. We believe that the fullest measure of freedom of expression-as the Leader of the Opposition said this morning when he spoke-and that all sides of shades of opinion ought to be heard. I think that is quite correct. I think I can speak for all of my colleagues-I know I can for myself-when I say that we have never at any time attempted to keep anyone from saying what he wanted to say. We have never at any time tried to keep anyone off the air, nor have we attempted at any time to deny anyone the right of the freedom to express himself.

I did not keep him off the air; I was objecting to what he was saying.

I think, Mr. Chairman, it is quite clear that we have never at any time done that. There have been objections made here in this house; there have been objections raised in committee concerning certain programs and certain types of programs; but at no time has any one of us ever attempted to keep anyone off the air.
I would like to impress on people's memories the fact that I was on a panel of discussion just a few years ago on the C.B.C. Trans-Canada network and the question that was under discussion then was whether the communists in this country should have the right to express their views over the C.B.C. network. I took the position then that they should, and I take that position now. They should not be denied the right of freedom of expression. Not at any time have we ever attempted to keep anyone off the air, and I just wanted to make that clear.
While we practise freedom of expression, we advocate the fullest possible measure of it, we are concerned about the ensurance that all sides of the question be given an opportunity for expression. We have criticized in this house and in the committee of parliament quite strongly what has appeared to us to be the neglect of a point of view or points of view or what has appeared to us to be suppression of points of view on very important questions which the people of Canada, we believe, had every right to hear. I do not believe that any one of my colleagues

has ever written to the chairman of the board of the C.B.C. protesting against a speaker. I think every protest that has ever been made by us has been made here or in the committee. If I am wrong, I would be happy to have anyone set me right. I know that I have never written the C.B.C. at any time, strongly as I have criticized some of their programs.
We feel that the C.B.C. is subject to the will of parliament, that is to the representatives of the people in this parliament, and quite rightly so because after all it is the people who pay the bills for the operation of the C.B.C. We feel that the members of parliament have every right to complain in parliament or in public, if they feel that there have been faults in C.B.C. programming or neglect or suppression; that is their right. The question arises, then, what about the Prime Minister? Has he the right to complain? I would say the Prime Minister, in every way, would have the same rights of ordinary individuals, the right to complain in this parliament or out of it if he feels that there has been some fault in C.B.C. programming. I would not attempt at all to deny him that right. I do not believe, however, that the Prime Minister or any of his government colleagues or indeed any group of members of the house, would have any right to interfere or attempt to interfere with C.B.C. programs.
If the C.B.C. is making some mistakes in programming, there is a way to get at them to have the matter corrected, even if we have to go so far as to remove from office certain people who have been at fault. I would certainly say, in spite of the fact we have no right to interfere and certainly that can be said of the government more than it could be of ordinary individuals, we do have a right to complain. I do not know what we shall have to call this particular incident, but I think I can understand something of what the Prime Minister was trying to get over to us this morning. I think he did indicate that one of his criticisms of the program under discussion was that here was a person appearing under one title and attempting to do something altogether different. I have seen that happen a good many times. To put it in specific terms, what happened appears to me to be an attempt at political interpretation when, as a matter of fact, the young man appeared on what was supposed to be an educational program. I have seen that happen time and time again. A person appears under one guise and then goes on and does something totally different.
I believe, as the Prime Minister expressed himself this morning, when anyone goes on the air to give any one of the commentaries

or for the purpose of expressing his opinions it should be definitely understood who is sponsoring him, what his background is and so on, so that the people will understand. I object strongly to having programs on the air that are not what they appear to be or what they have been advertised to be. I do not know whether or not that is what the Prime Minister had in his mind, but I would certainly think if a person is appearing on what is supposed to be an educational talk and then he turns it into a political interpretation, he is at fault and the people who put him there are at fault for not having made it abundantly clear that is what he was supposed to do. Now, that kind of thing is quite often done, as I say, but I should like to point out this important thing. The position in which Mr. Dunton finds himself today is an example of the kind of thing or at least an example of one of the prices we shall have to pay for having crown corporations. This is especially true of crown corporations that could be turned to propaganda purposes as it very often has.
I am not attempting here to place the blame on the C.C.F. for having brought this matter up, but I am going to say this as an example, that the C.C.F. has been very loud in its demands for crown corporations of all kinds. They have been the greatest defenders of the C.B.C., even when the C.B.C. has been at fault. They do not complain against the C.B.C., and there is good reason for it. They have no reason for complaining because the C.B.C. has favoured the leftist point of view right down the line, and that is one of the complaints we have had. They have undue emphasis toward the leftist point of view and have not balanced it with an opportunity for the right point of view to be presented.

I have criticized, Mr. Prime Minister, the C.B.C. right here in this house for having used the taxpayers' money for a purpose which I thought at the time, and I think I proved conclusively-while it may not have been the avowed purpose of the C.B.C.-did have the result of undermining our way of life at a time when we were gathering from the Canadian people huge amounts of taxation to fight communism; we were then spending the taxpayers' money to the tune of several thousands of dollars to give the communists comfort that could come to them from having a particular line emphasized over the whole C.B.C. network. I am just trying to impress on the minister the fact that I too have been criticized for having dared to bring up a question of that importance right on the floor of this house where it should be brought up and so I can quite understand how he might feel today.
I am not excusing him for one moment if indeed his actions can be interpreted as an attempt to interfere with the C.B.C. I do not think it was. It may have been a mistake; I do not know. Let us stand on the floor of this house or in the committee on radio broadcasting and criticize and complain about it all we like. Let us make certain that we follow a policy that

I am just pointing that out because it is done so often. That is about all I have to say, Mr. Chairman.

not think it could be taken that the Prime Minister was exercising a right of censorship. He has no right of censorship over C.B.C. programs but I think that he has, as anybody else has, a right to call attention to what he considers is not the best way to carry out the duties which I know the officials are trying to carry out in the manner they consider to be the best way. In this country it is fortunate that the Prime Minister does not have to be surrounded with the guards and other paraphernalia that accompany like positions in other countries. It is fortunate that the temper of the Canadian public is such that in Canada the Prime Minister can go about just as any other Canadian citizen.

Are we to take it that the Prime Minister would feel free to write a similar letter to Mr. Dunton again?

speechtext: I would not like to do anything that would be the occasion of the kind of field day we have had today and had I anticipated that it would bring about this kind of field day I would have-
Called him on the telephone.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: -concealed the irritation I felt at the supercilious tone of this broadcast.
Better call him on the telephone next time.

In other words, the Prime
Minister has had his lesson.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, I do not know if it is a lesson but there has been a demonstration of what use can be made of rather insignificant incidents.
Before the resolution carries, I have another grievance I should like to raise at this time unless someone wishes to carry on the debate that has been under way.

speechtext: Before my hon. friend leaves this subject, if he is changing the subject-

My grievance has to do-
The Depuiy Chairman: Order. The Leader of the Opposition suggests that he be permitted to follow the subject that has been under discussion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is one question on which we have not had any enlightenment. Apparently there was a suggestion by the Prime Minister that these commentators should be subject to a form of licence, that at least what they were going to say should be examined and their pedigrees considered to ensure that only the most authentic, dependable and authoritative observations might be made by those persons who would have the opportunity of speaking over this mass propaganda agency. We have not heard, however, the reaction of Mr. Dunton to all of this. How did he react? Did he give an undertaking that from now on the intonation of the voices of those who are to broadcast will receive a kind of preliminary run-off or that very close examination will be made from now on of those who are permitted to be commentators? Those are things we should know because I feel that a direction of that kind would certainly directly destroy the effectiveness of any person who acted the part of a commentator.

Interim Supply
I have disagreed with commentators on what they have said. I have certainly had strong views with regard to statements made, but if the C.B.C. is to remain an instrument for the independent propagation of thought my views are of no consequence any more than the views of the Prime Minister as a private citizen. I ask the Prime Minister this question. What did Mr. Dunton say in effect? Did he agree that the Prime Minister had the right to so direct? Did he raise any objection to what had been done? What was the nature of his reaction?
These are things that seem to remain in doubt. After all, one would naturally expect that Mr. Dunton would express some surprise that the Prime Minister should be endeavouring, either directly or by subtle suggestion, to determine the type of commentators who should be permitted to speak over the national broadcasting system.
What was his reaction? I am sure it would be most interesting to know his attitude, and whether or not he did not take a very strong stand against anything in the nature of interference with the thoughts, the identity or the pedigree of those who were going to speak to Canadians as commentators.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, I do not have just exactly what he said. For that reason he had been selected for this broadcast. In my reply I think I pointed out, that this comment was not known to the audience that was being spoken to, and that I thought it was unfortunate that there had not been some explanatory note to indicate that this was one point of view that the C.B.C. felt might be interesting to have heard, but that it was not an educational broadcast promoted by the C.B.C. as a part of its educational program.

Mr. Chairman, I would like the Prime Minister to tell us this. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This was before the Suez canal incident, Mir. Chairman, and therefore it was not so much the meaning of the broadcast that rather irritated me; it was the fact that a young man on a pedestal was looking down on these poor Canadians
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
