speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, I hope it will not, because from my knowledge and experience of young men, I expect whatever they say, whether it be over the radio or elsewhere, will be quite agreeable to my ears.
May I ask the Prime Minister whether from his reply to the Leader of the Opposition we are to understand that two letters were written by him to Mr. Dunton?
Yes. I said that yesterday, and I think I repeated it this morning. I wrote one letter; I received an answer from Mr. Dunton and I replied to his answer.
In his reply to the Prime Minister did Mir. Dunton address the letter to the Prime Minister at his private residence as a private citizen or did he send it to him as Prime Minister at the east block?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, that I really could not say, because on everything that is addressed to me at 24 Sussex street, the "24 Sussex street" has a lead pencil bar put through it and "east block" is written in, and it goes to the east block.
Mr. Chairman-

Before the hon. member changes the subject I wish to make this observation. I am not going to ask a question. I think this has been a rather healthy discussion and it will probably hinder anyone in the future from indicating not only on the radio and on television, but it might go farther than that and reach out to the press that certain people do not like certain things that might appear in the press. If that were done we would get censorship of all the articles that might appear in the press. I think this is a very healthy discussion and probably some warnings can be taken from it when we see what happens in European countries and other places.

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated earlier, I have a matter that I wish to bring before the committee. It has to do with the payment of subvention for coastal services on western local services to the Union Steamship Line, which is in direct competition with other lines which are not receiving the same consideration.
Unfortunately the information I have to present to the committee was not available to me when we were discussing the supplementary estimates for 1956-57, but I did get certain information which is relative to what the Minister of Finance discussed at page 2511 of Hansard when we had a similar item before us on March 20 of this year. I must, for purposes of clarifying the position I take, read from Hansard of that day. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the Minister of Finance had an exchange on the supplementary subvention of some $237,000. I note that in this year's estimates there is a similar item amounting to $325,000. At page 2511 the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked this question:
Have there been any applications from any other shipping firms for subventions for this route or part of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not sure. When they came
before the treasury board they had to satisfy the chairman that this was the only steamship company that could provide the service for which we are paying a subvention and that it was necessary having in mind the costs of the particular transportation system.
I have taken the time to discover whether or not there were any other steamship lines going into the region covered, and I find that the Union Steamship Lines have withdrawn their services from the Howe sound, Georgia straits and Johnstone straits area. On April 9 of this year they will withdraw their services from the west coast of Vancouver island. There are competing lines in the same area. Canadian Steamships carry both freight and passengers to one district, Ocean Falls, Kitimat, Prince Rupert, and Ketchikan, Alaska, in lower west coast ports of Vancouver island, and they also operate a daily service to the lower east coast of Vancouver island. Canadian National Steamship Lines has a service in the summer to Ocean Falls, Kitimat, Prince Rupert and the Canadian Pacific Steamship Lines jointly with the Canadian National during the rest of the year.
The island tug and barge will, from April 9, 1957, provide service to the north end of the west coast of Vancouver island. The Northland Navigation Company Limited has four freight vessels a week to Alert bay and
Interim Supply
points north to Prince Rupert, and it now operates a freight vessel for all points to Haines, including Stewart.
The Packers Steamship Company provides service to the Queen Charlotte islands and other northern points.
Those are the companies, Mr. Chairman, which carry the bulk of the service and the passengers without a subsidy, that is other than Union Steamship Lines. We find that Union Steamship Lines is reducing its freight rate and is going into these same ports. This is a fact that must be kept in mind. I believe that the reason, in part at least, for the subsidy is the fact that Union Steamship carries passengers into the Stewart area once every two weeks, Graham island once every two weeks and Bella Coola once every week.
I find on investigation that Union Steamship Lines is not offering an alternate service. The ports of call for Union Steamship Lines are the same as the ports of call for some of these other companies with the exception of those three additional points. I have here a map on which I have outlined the routes of these companies and the ports at which Union Steamship Lines calls. For instance, in the general area of Ocean Falls and Bella Coola, we have the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and Union Steamships going into Ocean Falls. Not too far away at Bella Coola, although some distance by sea, is the Union Steamships weekly service. We find at another point, at Stewart, the Union Steamship Lines carries on by itself.
As I indicated earlier, I find that Union Steamship Lines is in competition with Northland Navigation and the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific at Kitimat. Still another point is Prince Rupert where we find the Canadian Pacific, Northland and the C.P.R. as well as the Union Steamship Lines in competition.
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, and I think it has become apparent, in the past year we have given a subsidy of $562,000 to Union Steamship Lines to carry passengers into three ports and their service is merely an extension of the service from some of these other points. I find on further investigation that this same Union Steamship Lines borrowed $2 million on December 29, 1955, at a secured rate of interest of 5 per cent, to enable certain of its directors to purchase the controlling shares of the company formerly held by the Canadian Pacific and certain small shareholders.
Now I contend, sir, that if this company were in a position to borrow money to distribute to shareholders in order to purchase shares from the Canadian Pacific and other small shareholders, then they did not need to come to the government of Canada for a subsidy in order to carry on operations and

Interim Supply
at the same time reduce freight rates while they are competing with other lines which are interested in doing this business. The fact is that there are some 158,521 shares, the bulk of which numbering 147,855 are owned by Senator S. S. McKeen and Mr. F. B. Brown and associates.
In my opinion it does seem a very serious state of affairs when the parliament of this country is proposing to subsidize a company which, as I said earlier, provides such a limited service on routes that are practically all covered by other competing lines which are not asking for a subsidy. Under those circumstances, before we pass any item of the estimates in this connection, I would suggest that the minister set up a public hearing to be held on the west coast and have all authorities make representations before we decide to pass another such subvention. If that were not done, then I would hope there would be a call for tenders to see whether or not we could get the service at a figure lower than $562,000 from one of these other firms which are in the legitimate business of carrying passengers in that general area and who would be prepared to do that for us.

I have a matter which I feel to be of considerable importance to many of my constituents. Hon. members might recall that on February 19 I directed questions to the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance dealing with the matter. It had also been brought to the attention of the house by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I refer, of course, to bulletin 10 of the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, dated July 10, 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt on a point of order. In this debate I think it is permissible for hon. members to discuss quite a wide variety of subjects. However, there is before the house a resolution having to do with income tax, and my hon. friend could discuss this particular point on that but not on this. I would not want to say, if the resolution were not before the house, he would not be in order at the moment. But when a resolution is there dealing with income tax, a debate of this kind I suggest should not take place. On this debate he should not refer to other matters that can be debated, for the reason I have given.

While I appreciate the position taken by the minister, it was not my intention to go into a detailed examination of this particular matter. This can be done at a later time. I do feel there is urgency here in that a number of constituents have communicated with me with reference to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They have also communicated with me and every other member of the house has received similar representations- at least, I assume so. Urgency is not a reason for breaking the rules when a debate can properly take place on some other matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I wonder if perhaps I could be of some slight help to the committee by pointing out that when one hon. member referred to the fact he had a grievance to bring up at the time the last one was exhausted, we were not on the open motion that Mr. Speaker leave the chair at which time grievances are brought up. Those matters can cover any subject of federal jurisdiction.
However, we are now in committee of supply discussing a resolution which includes every item in the estimates, but it does not include any item of taxation. We are not in ways and means; we are not raising the money, we are spending it. I could not rule out of order any discussion such as the last member brought up because it dealt with a subsidy included in the estimates and at this time we are voting one-twelfth of it. But if the hon. member is proposing to discuss something other than the expenditure of public funds under the estimates in this resolution, he would not be in order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask a question of you, sir, and of the minister. Does it not turn on whether or not this bulletin No. 10 is a matter of legislation that is covered in the minister's resolutions or whether it is a matter of administration paid for out of the administration item of the Department of National Revenue. It seems to me it is the latter which is in order now. On the other hand, if it is covered by one of the resolutions of the Minister of Finance there is validity to his point. Can he tell me which it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, there is no question at all that direotive 10 is an administrative directive, as far as that goes, but in supply as I understand it we are discussing the expenditure of moneys. This is not a case of being able to discuss any matter which is on the order paper. If it were we would have two debates about the same subject.
Now, I know my hon. friend is not going to give me an engagement when he completes this speech that neither he nor any other hon. member will speak on directive 10 when we get to the Income Tax Act, because obviously he could not do that. What I am saying is that my hon. friend will discuss it now and will discuss it again on the resolution on income tax, and for that reason he cannot have it twice. He must have it once, and that in its proper place.

My interpretation was as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that this is a question of administration. Someone in the department directed that a bulletin go out to the various offices across the country. It was not a question of legislation or an amendment to the Income Tax Act. It is simply a matter of internal administration within the department itself.
In view of the urgency of the matter I felt that I would like to urge swifter action on the part of the government, because there have been answers given to hon. members in this house regarding consideration being given to this matter but to date we have not seen any results. There are many people in my constituency who are eagerly awaiting a decision on this important matter.
Having said that I will leave this matter in abeyance until a later date, but I will want to explain the reason I thought it proper to bring up this matter at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you very much.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is a matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Department of National Revenue, and that is the need of action being taken to keep open the port of West Poplar, Saskatchewan, from 9 a.m. until 10 p.m. This is not a local matter but one that concerns the extent of tourist traffic from the United States that ordinarily would be available to parts of northern Saskatchewan, including Waskesiu park and the Lac la Ronge area and north. In recent years United States tourists have been entering the province of Saskatchewan in increasing numbers bringing a source of wealth that is vitally necessary to the economy.
This port is the entry for travellers using highway No. 2, which is the main south-north route in Saskatchewan, going right up the centre of the province for a total distance of 475 miles, and serving the province's main tourist areas. The highway itself serves as the main tourist highway. The Americans who enter Saskatchewan do so on that new highway north of Glasgow, Montana, from Opheim to the border, which is a direct route leading to No. 2 highway in the province of Saskatchewan. The international No. 2 highway association through the president of its Canadian section, Mr. E. J. Goos, has petitioned the department on previous occasions to keep the facilities of this port open in order to encourage increased use by tourists of the facilities that are available in Saskatchewan. The hours during which the port is kept open constitute a discrimination 82715-180
Interim Supply
against the province of Saskatchewan as compared to the ports east of this port, in the province of Manitoba, and west of it in the province of Alberta.
Between the Manitoba border and Regway, a distance of 140 miles, there are seven ports of entry each of which is open until 10 p.m. or later, but between Regway and the Alberta border, a distance of some 235 miles, not one of the six ports of entry is open beyond 6 p.m. In other words, the eastern one-third of the international line in Saskatchewan has seven entry ports open after 6 p.m., whereas the other two-thirds have not a single one open after 6 p.m.
It may be argued that the number of tourists who enter through this port does not warrant the additional hours, but the fact is that the reason adjacent ports show a larger tourist entry is simply that after 6 p.m. it is impossible for tourists to use the West Poplar port of entry, and therefore they enter through ports east or west of it.
None of the other ports has available the same highways that cross at this particular port. Highway No. 2 is the main highway into Saskatchewan.
I simply rise for the purpose of supporting the application that has been made by the international No. 2 highway association, that between June 1 and September 15 this port be kept open as are the ports to the east and west of it after 6 p.m. and until 10 p.m. I do not want to say anything further in this regard. It is not in any way a personal matter but something which concerns the entire province of Saskatchewan. The province has provided tremendous facilities for tourists, and should not be discriminated against because entry is denied to prospective United States tourists by reason of the closing hour at this port being four hours earlier than the closing hour of adjacent ports.
In northern Saskatchewan we have some of the finest fishing facilities available anywhere in Canada. Each year many tourists from the United States go to the Lac la Ronge district and those areas north of it, and many go to the national park at Waskesiu. I ask the minister, in order to encourage the expansion and continued development in that direction, that representations be made by him to the Minister of National Revenue to assure that this port will be kept open in order to encourage to the greatest possible degree the entry of additional tourists into Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall draw the attention of the Minister of National Revenue to the remarks made by my hon. friend, Mr. Chairman.

Interim Supply
One finds oneself in a rather difficult position on an occasion like this, having only the Minister of Finance and three other ministers present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not want to say the Minister of Finance appreciates that as anything more than a good joke, because looking back on the eight or nine years during which I have been paying attention to these matters, (a) I have never seen a debate of this length, and (b) I have never seen ministers of the crown being cross-examined. There may have been instances when this was done but I do not recall them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And (c), the Prime Minister never wrote a letter to Mr. Dunton before.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be misunderstood. I was not taking exception to the fact that when we have interim supply it is usual for the Minister of Finance to pilot these things through, if that is the proper term to use. My comment was not intended in any way as a reflection upon the fact that other ministers might not be here at this particular moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Look around you; you have no one. Look at the number of members present on that side.
What is the percentage?

Mr. Chairman, I did not propose to occupy very much time. I did not say what I said with the idea of casting any reflection. To make my intention perfectly clear I want to say that I have some questions to ask the Minister of National Defence, and I can certainly ask the questions now if I decide to do so. I was merely indicating that it would have been much better all the way around if I had the opportunity of directing my questions to the Minister of National Defence. That is all I was getting at.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I only interrupted for this purpose, and I am sure I do not take my hon. friend's remarks in ill part at all. I only say that I do not recall an occasion since I have been paying attention to these things, either during my time or in my predecessor's time when it was the custom to ask questions of a minister during interim supply. There may be general argument that at the particular moment there should be some discussion on a public matter for the purpose of putting it on the record at a time which suits the convenience of hon. members opposite, but I have never known the motion for interim supply to be considered the occasion for something in the nature of an inquiry about the estimates as such, and I think that is what my hon. friend has in mind.

May I point this out to keep the record straight. We are faced with quite a different situation than has been the case on previous occasions when we were asked to vote interim supply. During the past number of years it has been customary, even commonplace, for us to reach this particular time in the fiscal year when it became obvious that in order to carry on, let us say for the month of April, the minister would have to come before us and ask for one-twelfth of the estimates. On those occasions the minister has given, as he did today, the assurance that members of parliament in no way would be restricted as far as the consideration of the main estimates was concerned.
Let us not forget that this is not the same situation we had last year or the year before. We are being asked for one-twelfth of the estimates for the fiscal year 1957-58. Within the course of let us say 10 days or two weeks we may be asked for another one-twelfth of the estimates, but it is conceivable that we may not have an opportunity to consider the budget resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have given assurances to hon. gentlemen opposite that as far as I am concerned they will.

The only way the minister could really give that assurance would be to assure all hon. members that they will be coming back. With all its assurances it is quite conceivable that the government could proceed to finance for another eight or ten months without any hon. member of this house having an opportunity to say very much, if anything, about how the amounts listed in the estimates are to be spent.
Possibly I should not have said at the beginning that I intended to cross-examine a particular minister, but I suggest that conceivably it might have been better if the Minister of National Defence had an opportunity to make a short statement with respect to what I am going to say.
I could not help but note when the main estimates were tabled, and again when announcements were made to the house with respect to certain contemplated expenditures, let us say in the field of health and social services, that emphasis seemed always to be placed on the fact that we were facing an extreme inflationary danger. Reference was always made to the possible effects of increasing certain expenditures upon that inflationary condition.
I have watched closely for some comment with respect to the largest single item of expenditure in our budget, namely the 35

cents out of every dollar which is allocated to national defence. Over $1,722 million are being allocated for national defence during this coming fiscal year, a reduction of approximately $52 million or 3 per cent compared with the estimates of last year. But I would remind the committee that on top of that we have over $16 million for the Department of Defence Production, and many of the allocations for the Department of External Affairs and other departments could be categorized as appropriations for national defence.
It seems significant that during the last three or four weeks I have received quite a number of communications either criticizing the government or asking why it is that the government does not get right down to business and effect essential economies in the field of national defence. It is pointed out in one document I have received that all collections in the personal income tax field and one-third of the collections in the sales tax field are required to cover the appropriations for the Department of National Defence.
It is pointed out that while Canada is spending 35 per cent of its tax and non-tax revenue on national defence the United States spends only 11 per cent and Great Britain, which has borne a terrific burden and which has just as much at stake as we have, spends only 9 per cent. The general feeling on the part of the government there is that that percentage is far too high, and they must make certain reductions without affecting the defence of the nation. Denmark spends 3.6 per cent of its budget on national defence.
I might just say at this point that while so much attention is being paid to the necessity of holding the line as far as health services are concerned-I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare would be probably the first to point out that his department uses about 2 cents of the revenue dollar-while the Department of Agriculture uses about 2 cents out of every revenue dollar; while the Department of Public Works uses 4 cents and the Department of Veterans Affairs 5 cents; while our provincial subsidies require 8 cents out of every tax dollar; while we use 9 cents to cover family allowances, 11 cents for public debt interest, and 20 cents for all other expenditures exclusive of national defence, we find we are expending 35 cents out of every dollar for national defence.
We in this group have always taken the position-we took it during the war and ever since-that Canada must have adequate 82715-180*
Interim Supply
defences, but there is increasing evidence that Canada can secure those adequate defences at a lesser cost. There is plenty of evidence to indicate that. I shall not take the time to go into detail, though I could produce the evidence at the present time.
The Minister of Finance, acting in the best interests of the Canadian people, should see to it that there is a clamping down soon as far as that department is concerned. I contend that this department contributes more to the inflationary condition we have today than any other department of government. In the first place, there is no department of government which makes such claims on our capital resources. There is no department of government that makes such a heavy claim upon consumer goods. There is no department of government that makes a proportionately greater claim upon manpower, both skilled and unskilled. This department enters into strong competition with the civilian market, and makes it very difficult for the civilian market because of the extremely high inducements which are offered to those who go into this particular field.
It is also probably true that there is no other department of government of which it can be said that its activities are directly concerned with the providing of services, and very wonderful and valuable services at that. But practically all wages, all pensions, all gratuities, salaries and so on, provide direct competition for the consumer goods of the nation.
I am wondering whether economies which might be desirable in the Department of National Defence are left to the Department of National Defence itself to decide. I am inclined to believe the time has come when the government of Canada should see to it that a body quite outside the Department of National Defence is given this responsibility. I do not think the treasury board would be good enough in this particular case, though it does good work in the field in which it operates.
What I have in mind is that we should get right down to home base to see whether or not it is possible to ensure an adequate defence for Canada, but at the same time chop 10 or 15 per cent off the cost. Some of those who live in areas where defence establishments exist have approached me within recent times and have given me information indicating that there could well be a tightening up in a number of directions; for example, with regard to the utilization of armed service vehicles for non-military purposes. These people know this is being done, and they know what these vehicles are being used for.

Interim Supply
Such matters may sound unimportant, but I am definitely inclined to believe that if a body such as I have suggested were to study the situation they could make some very useful recommendations. The government so far has shown no reluctance to set up royal commissions of various kinds. We have had bodies appointed to inquire into radio and television, the arts and sciences and so forth, and I am inclined to believe the time has arrived when we should appoint somebody to ascertain whether or not we get service in return for money spent, and whether it is necessary to spend more than about 60 per cent of what is being spent today in order to get the same type of defence protection.
Mr. Chairman, I do not expect that a cabinet minister can be everywhere and know everything that is going on, no matter how capable, how honest or how reliable he may be. This is no reflection upon the minister. As a matter of fact I am almost inclined to believe he would not mind following a course such as I have suggested. And I am urging on my own behalf, as a member of parliament, and on behalf of those who see a good many things going on and who have reported them to me, that the government should give some consideration to taking the course of action I have proposed.
In case it may be said that I have said either too much or not enough, may I point out that I am in a position to elaborate to some extent, and I may even do so. However, Mr. Chairman, I think I have opened the door, and there are a lot of members of this house who will be able to support what I say from their own experience and from evidence which has come to them. What I have said is no reflection on the individual members of the armed services, and I do not want anyone to say it is. That is not what I am saying at all. It is something resulting, maybe, from certain accepted courses of procedure. However, I would certainly like to see some action taken in connection with the matter.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I explained to hon. members privately yesterday that I had another public engagement this afternoon, and I am now over two hours late. Potatoes are coming in from the United States at a price which makes it impossible to obtain a market for the local product. Down home they are being peddled from house to house. speechtext: 334. Operations-including salaries and other expenses of staff post offices, district offices, railway mail service staffs, and supplies, equipment and other items for revenue post offices, also including administration, $93,819,562.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the Postmaster General one question. As found at page 2023 of Hansard of March 8, the minister mentioned that he had received assurances from the manufacturers of the electronic equipment for the sorting machine, and that the installation would start by March 29. Can the minister tell us whether that has happened?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I did say that March 29 was the date I had been informed that they would start installation. I am told that the machine is being shipped this week end and that installation of the machine in the Ottawa post office will start on Monday.

There is a matter I should like to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General. On a previous occasion I made some reference to the question of mail delivery service in the city of Regina, and suggested that there should be a speed-up in the service. Since that time I have had the opportunity of examining the status of mail delivery in certain sections of the city. While assurances have been given that delivery services are to be extended to sections where they are not now in existence, there is one particular area of the city I should like to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General.
I have recently received a communication from a constituent living in a housing area in the city of Regina known as Pioneer Village. This is a housing development for senior citizens of the city of Regina. At the present time the dwellings house somewhere in the neighbourhood of 170 people, all of whom are either old age pensioners or spouses of old age pensioners. At the present time they are not receiving delivery service to their homes, and I think of all people who deserve consideration with respect to the delivery of mail it should be our senior citizens.
Some of these people find it very difficult to go to the central office in order to collect their mail, and in view of the age of the people living in Pioneer Village I think special consideration should be given to them. I would ask the minister whether it might not be possible for the department to provide delivery service to the homes which these people occupy.

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I will be very pleased to look into the situation. I might tell my hon. friend that I happen to know the particular locality. When Pioneer Village was developed I was made acquainted with the development in my other capacity as Minister of Veterans Affairs, and I will certainly look into the matter.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister while we are dealing with the transportation vote. I think I can best illustrate the point I have in mind by reading briefly from a letter I received recently from one of my constituents. The letter reads in part as follows:
As you know we get a weekly boat which brings mail and supplies, no passenger service at all. But my complaint is over the mail. It takes two weeks to get a reply from Vancouver now. When the Union boat carried our mails we could order stuff from Vancouver by one boat and get it delivered on the next boat up. Now it always takes two weeks and even urgent letters take two weeks for an answer and three weeks from Campbell River to here. There is something sloppy somewhere. I wish you would give someone a kick where it would do the most good.
I am going on the assumption that this is the proper place to do the kicking. I can give the minister the particulars of the locality to which I am referring, but the complaint I have in mind is of more general application. By way of illustration I would remind the minister that this letter makes reference to the fact that it takes three weeks to deliver a letter from Read Island to Campbell River.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: What is the locality?

This letter comes from Read Island, but the writer mentions that it takes three weeks to get a letter from Read Island to Campbell River. Read Island by air from Campbell River is approximately ten minutes flight. Read Island is located in part of the school district centred on Campbell River. It is part of the hospital administration district centred on the hospital at Campbell River, and generally speaking Campbell River is the main centre for this area. I have mentioned that it is about ten minutes by air from Campbell River to the place where my correspondent lives.
I think situations of this kind perhaps do illustrate the need for the department to review some of its existing policy in respect of those whom it allows to carry the mail. As

I understand it, generally speaking arrangements for the carrying of the mail are made only with scheduled air lines, but as I see the situation developing in the coastal areas of British Columbia we now have quite a number of what amounts almost to scheduled services but which are actually on a non-scheduled air charter basis. Perhaps the department could profitably examine the possibility in some cases of making exceptions to the policy which requires that scheduled air lines carry the mails. That is particularly true in cases where, within the limits of a few days, arrangements could be worked out so mails could be delivered on a much more frequent time schedule on a reasonable cost basis than the one now existing with the boat service on some parts of the coast.
I use this particular situation as an example because we have an air base at Campbell River. It happens to be operated by a firm known as British Columbia Air Lines, which operates small light planes that, in the course of a week, visit most of the places in the area which generally find an administrative and shopping centre in Campbell River.
It is unfortunate that people who live that close to a centre of that kind have to be confined to a mail service every three weeks from one place to the other. I hope the department will make a careful review of this situation, because I feel it might well be possible to work out some variation in existing plans and regulations that would provide some of these people with a much better service than they are getting at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the people served by R.R. 1, Kakabeka Falls, I wish to thank the Postmaster General and his officials for a six-day a week delivery instead of a thrice weekly delivery. The people appreciate it and asked me to extend their appreciation. They use their mail in a proper way, too.
Is the minister in a position to answer my question of last week regarding the mail contracts with T.C.A., C.P.A., the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the cost of the conveyance of mails during the last calendar year-I have the figures for one year back, as my hon. friend may understand. From December 1, 1955, to November, 1956, they are as follows: Canadian Pacific Railway, $5,753,163.67; Canadian National Railway, $7,029,020.42; T.C.A., $8,759,594.25; Canadian Pacific Air Lines, $1,769,830.67.

Can the minister now bring us up to date as to the intentions of the department in relation to the parcel post delivery

service for the Vancouver-Burnaby-New Westminster area? Exactly what plans has the department in mind at the present time?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There has been no change in the situation to date, Mr. Chairman.
Do I take from the hon. minister's reply that conditions will remain as they now exist until at least the end of 1957?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily, Mr. Chairman. We are looking into the situation from the point of view of bringing in a system which will be more efficient and more economical than the present system.

Can the minister inform us what the per parcel delivery cost is to the post office of the business handled by the pony express? Is it 11 cents per parcel or 16 cents per parcel, or what does it work out at?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: They are not on an item basis; they are on an hourly basis. The plan we are looking into at the present time is to establish a per item basis for those contracts through the whole postal area of Vancouver for the purpose of getting a better control and a more efficient and a more economical delivery system, but this has not yet been accomplished.

Can the minister tell us what the hourly rate is to the pony express? I have seen some of the pay statements. I know that while they pay on an hourly basis, they also make a calculation of how much this is costing on a per item basis. I would like to know what is the hourly rate?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is $2.95 an hour.
Can the minister tell us what it works out to on a per parcel basis? I know the department does furnish that.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Slightly over 12 cents.

The minister says they are investigating a scheme which would put the whole thing on a per item basis, and I wish to commend the economy efforts that are being actively considered. In the light of the minister's announced policy of decentralization, can he assure us that when these new arrangements are decided upon tenders will be called at least for those parcel post areas that are now being serviced by the pony express? Will tenders be called for the New Westminster and South Burnaby areas when and if the new arrangement is arrived at?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
If tenders are called for, Mr. Chairman, they will be for contracts to cover the whole postal area of Vancouver. One of the purposes of this project is to avoid having to deal in parcel post delivery with 8, 10, 15 or 20 different contractors, all operating on
Supply-Post Office
different bases. Purely from an efficient and economical point of view we believe, and the officials of the department advise me, that in such postal areas as Vancouver the operation should be one single operation, so to speak, and that is what we are looking into now. I am advised that such an operation would be both more efficient and more economical, but no final decision has been taken yet.

I understand that at one time an offer was made to take on at least one of those units at a per item cost of less than the present cost being paid to the pony express. I do not think the minister has quite made clear to us how this fits in with his announced policy of decentralization.
I do not see what difference it makes to the New Westminster postmaster whether parcels are being serviced by a New Westminster man under contract or whether it is some outside firm coming in from Vancouver to pick up the parcels. I wonder whether the minister could be a little clearer so we could really understand him when he says he is pursuing a policy of decentralization, and he now tells us it is more efficient to have it all under one roof, as it were.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
When I have referred
previously to the policy of decentralization I have always had in mind the recommendations which were contained in the Woods-Gordon report to the effect that decentralization should be put into effect in the Post Office Department. What was meant there was that the over-all control from headquarters in Ottawa should be decentralized to the various postal districts. In other words it was felt the heads of these various districts should be given more authority to deal with local problems as they came up. This has been done, and the practice is being continued. It is that to which I referred as the decentralization policy.
Now, one could go on with decentralization until you get down to the individual operation or each individual employee of the department, but a certain control has to be exercised at one level, and we are now doing that at the district level.
Would the minister care to commit himself on that subject and state whether a city like Saskatoon is an efficient operating unit, or would it be too small a unit for efficient postal operation?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, but I do not understand.

The minister was making a point that we could carry this decentralization to the point of ridiculousness, and I agree with him. We cannot decentralize down to the

Supply-Post Office
last employee. However, I am fully aware of the fact, first of all, that there are possibly thousands of post offices which serve only 75 or 100 households. They may be uneconomic from a business standpoint, but I should like to have a statement from the minister as to whether a city of 50,000 or 60,000 like Saskatoon would be an efficient unit, and whether you could follow the policy of decentralization down at least that far.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Saskatoon, as I understand it, is a unit by itself and under its jurisdiction may come some adjacent territories. It is considered that it should operate as a unit. We have in Saskatoon, as elsewhere, local officials who now have greater authority to deal with problems without necessarily having to wait for a decision from headquarters. They have more authority than they had previously.

The minister is familiar with my representations to him in respect to the same contract we are discussing. I would ask him now whether the pony express has a firm contract at this time covering the whole metropolitan area of Vancouver.

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.
Then the minister spoke of an investigation that is being undertaken. When does he expect a report on that investigation?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, the study has been pretty well completed, Mr. Chairman, but no decision has been taken yet.

In view of the fact the department is in the process of making a decision, can the minister let us know when he expects the decision will be made known as to what method is going to be used, and who is to get the contract?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to answer that exactly.

The fact is, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam indicated a few moments ago, that there is a group in the city of New Westminster interested in the opportunity of bidding on this over-all service. Will they be given an opportunity to tender on the distribution of parcel post mail in the metropolitan area, the same as pony express?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Well, if tenders are invited for a system covering the whole area they will have an opportunity to tender for the whole operation the same as anyone else.

Do we have assurance, then, that tenders will be called before any action is
[Mr. Regier.l
taken in respect to who shall receive the contract, that is the whole contract?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, before any contract would be awarded.
In that case, could the minister explain how it was that these men received their notice without tenders being called for the whole contract?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Because these men did not have a contract with the department. I explained that previously. Each of them had what is known, and what they know, as a temporary arrangement. It was simply an agreement between the local responsible officer and these men to do that work on the basis of so much an hour. This agreement could be terminated at any time.
That is a practice which has always been followed by the department in dealing with these contracts in large centres, particularly before tenders for a firm contract are called. Because of the various adjustments that have to be made, the practice of the department has been to enter into a temporary agreement and at a later date, based on the experience they have had with this temporary agreement, they can then make the basis for a firm contract.

There is much more involved than merely the parcel post delivery. It is very obvious that we are being asked to sacrifice our identities all around Vancouver just to build a political machine in the city of Vancouver. I would like you to call it five o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

All right, I will ask my question. I would like to know if there has been any correspondence with the provincial governments that are mentioned, in view of the fact that the schedules to this act cite certain statutes of the former province of Canada and the present provinces of Quebec and Ontario. This is a rather unique piece of legislation in that it amends a statute which was originally passed by the former province of Canada -prior to 1867-and was subsequently amended in part by the province of Ontario and in part by the province of Quebec. Now the federal parliament comes into the picture.
Private Bills

maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might attempt to answer my hon. friend's question, because I served as chairman of the committee which dealt with this bill. Those questions were asked in the committee and were replied to, I believe, by Mr. Addy, who was the counsel representing the order, and by the hon. member who sponsored the bill.
This order received their rights under the statutes of two different provinces many years ago and for some time they have been doing business, entering into contracts, performing various activities and have owned land. Throughout this period they have endeavoured to satisfy what they understood was the law of both the provinces from which they received their authority. I believe Mr. Addy indicated that the purpose of this bill was to re-establish the order as a proper legal entity, and that this in no way would affect the propriety of what they had done before. I do not know whether I have made myself clear to the hon. member.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, it still seems to me a rather odd situation. As the hon. member has pointed out, the statutes of two provinces of the present Dominion of Canada are involved, namely the statutes of the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario, but before 1867 and before those provinces came into being under the present British North America Act there existed the former province of Canada, and it was the legislative assembly of that original province of Canada which passed this statute in the first place.
What puzzles me is this. The original statute-in fact it is referred to in this act as the principal act-was amended by these two provinces that are now part of the Dominion of Canada, and I presume those amending statutes passed by Ontario and Quebec are included in the statutes of those provinces. Yet we have sections of this bill which amend and in fact repeal some sections of those provincial statutes.
I would like to know whether the provinces were consulted. I confess that this is a technical question, but, it does seem to me that it should be properly answered.

maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee it was I who asked Mr. Addy if there was any conflict between the provisions of the act we are now considering and the act to which the hon. gentleman refers, and his answer was in the negative, so I presume he had taken whatever steps were necessary.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext:
Well, whom did Mr. Addy represent?

Private Bills

maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext: He was the parliamentary agent.

maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is out of the ordinary for any entity that holds property or does business in various provinces to apply for a charter, as in this case, by act of parliament to establish their authority with the federal government, because it permits them to transact business interprovincially with greater facility.
I think there is sufficient advertising in government publications of bills of this nature to ensure that any objection that might be brought forward would be advanced. In the committee and in correspondence dealing with this matter it has not come to my attention that there is any objection. No objection to this act being approved was raised by any member of the committee, and the committee recommended it for the approval of the house.

maintopic: LES REVERENDS PERES OBLATS DE L'lMMACULEE CONCEPTION DE MARIE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have something to say applying both to clause 4 and clause 5. I do not intend to oppose this bill in any way, and I want to apologize to the chairman of the committee which considered this bill for not being able to attend. The clause reads:
The corporation may purchase, take, have, hold, receive, possess, retain and enjoy property, real or personal, corporeal, or incorporeal-
I read carefully the preceding clause to which the committee has just agreed, and I must compliment this corporation upon its objects. I remember a few years ago when another religious organization came to the miscellaneous private bills committee with an act of incorporation. I made careful note of one of the clauses in that bill. I refer to the bill which was brought to us a few years ago by the seventh day adventists.
This particular clause provided that if any real estate came into the possession of or was purchased by the corporation, unless it was used for the purposes for which it had been bought the directors were obligated to dispose of it within a specified time, which I believe in that case was 15 years. After the committee had met I met the clergyman who had attended the meeting out in the corridor

and told him I was pleased to see that clause in their act of incorporation, that it was something to be heartily endorsed. He told me they had looked over the acts of incorporation of a number of other religious organizations which had been given the blessing of parliament, and had simply copied the clause found therein word for word.
Quite often people bequeath real estate to religious organizations, and in older parts of the western world this has created certain evils in that the real estate has not been disposed of and at times had been permitted to become slum areas. Quite often religious organizations are hesitant about ridding themselves of real estate as long as it produces revenue, and religious organizations are always short of revenue.
I notice that this organization is doing a great variety of good works, I suppose throughout Quebec and Ontario, and I imagine that its funds are also limited. I wish some of our older religious organizations-I use the plural here because I have no particular church in mind-would consider the possibility of inserting a provision in their acts of incorporation which would ensure that real estate coming into their hands would be used only for the purpose of fulfilling the worthwhile objects of the organization, and that unless that is done the management would be directed to dispose of such holdings.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, March 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 15, respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company-Mr. Fairey-Mr. Robinson (Sim-coe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Subdivision of shares.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this measure was before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, after the officers of the company had spent most of the day with the committee the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond moved that clause 1 of the said bill be amended by deleting the word "five" in line 11 thereof and substituting therefor the word "ten", and by deleting the words "twenty millions" in line 14 and substituting therefor the words "fifty millions".
The members of our group could not support that amendment, but it is significant that several members on the government side were so dissatisfied with the proposal that they wished to register their objection in some way. There was a recorded vote and I find that Messrs. Casselman, Follwell,
Private Bills
Goode, Green, Kickham and Mclvor all voted for the amendment. It would appear that there were two Conservatives and four Liberals who felt they should register their objection before the bill was passed. When the amendment was defeated and the final vote was called Messrs. Barnett, Cameron (Nanaimo), Campbell, Johnston (Bow River), Nicholson and Thomas registered their objection.
I think it is significant that not a member on the government side of the house, apart from the sponsor of the bill, has stood up in parliament and attempted to say a good word for the proposal. I find that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond made a speech on March 13, 1953, in which he made some very critical remarks regarding the operations of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. I find that you, Mr. Chairman, had something to say when you were a member of the committee back in 1951. I find that you put these questions to the legal agent of the company:
Q. I understand your present intention is that the line shall end at Vancouver?
A. That is correct.
Q. Are you at the present time considering any plans for an extension of the line from Vancouver to Portland or Seattle or other places?
A. No, it is our intention to go to a terminal at Vancouver.
Q. You have no plans and you have not considered taking the line further south in the states?
A No, our present plans are entirely with respect to the bulk terminal at Vancouver, other arrangements being in the future.
Q. You will find the necessary refinery capacity at Vancouver?
A. That, you appreciate, will be the responsibility or the undertaking of the different refining companies. There will undoubtedly be refinery expansion concurrent with pipe line construction, but what the refinery companies' plans are I am not m a position to say.
The hon. member for Skeena is also on the record. He asked Mr. Blair this question: Will this Trans Mountain company be in the business of buying and selling oil or just carrying oil for other people?
Mr. Blair answered:
Its primary purpose is to carry oil.
In his speech on March 13, 1953, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond said:
[DOT] * * I believe that this house and the people of Canada may have occasion to request that this charter be reinvestigated.
On March 19, 1951, Mr. Blair, who was introduced to the committee as the parliamentary agent for the company, made the very definite commitment that the plans were that this would be an all-Canadian operation, that they had plenty of funds in Canada to finance it, that there was a market in Canada for the product at the west coast and that the building of the pipe line would result in a great development in the constituency of the hon.

Private Bills
member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and possibly in part of the riding of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.
What do we find now? We now find that more than half of the oil passing through the pipe line is going to the United States market.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
The sponsor says it is not true, but if he listened to the evidence given to the members of the committee he will recall that the estimates for 1957 indicate that more than half the oil passing through the pipe line will go to the United States market. I cannot take the time to look it up now but I am sure some of my colleagues will look up the information and give it to me. It will indicate that more than half of the oil is going to the United States market.
I submit that the hon. member who is sponsoring the measure should rise at some time while the bill is still before us to give some explanation to his colleagues who were prepared to pass the bill through parliament without even looking at the evidence which was placed before the committee that spent a day in interviewing the officials. Therefore I think it is pretty obvious that here is a *corporation that got the permission of parliament to build a pipe line under false prefences. They indicated that this was to be a project of which Canada could be proud, but now they are more concerned about the United States market than about Canada. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond asked this question, as found at page 34 of the proceedings of the committee:
Q. And June, please. I do not think X should ask you to go further than June.
A. June, 74,000 Canadian; 76,000 Washington; 49,000 tankers.
I am sure the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) has that information on page 34 of the evidence. The question was asked by his own colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. It was also admitted that the bulk of the 49,000 barrels of oil for tankers was for United States use. Therefore I submit that more than half the oil going through the pipe line is going to the United States.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Don't you believe in export?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I think it is very important that we export, but I also think it is very important that we give consideration to the use of Canadian resources in Canada to the maximum degree and the providing of employment for Canadians.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: What do you want to do with the oil? It is there.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I also believe we should call a halt to the building up of these large

U.S. corporations. Before the committee the officers of the company made it very clear that they did not need this legislation passed by parliament in order to get additional capital.
In 1951 they were given permission to issue 5 million shares, and to date they have issued less than one-third of that number, about 1,500,000. It is alleged that they want this legislation passed to have more people participate, and before our committee they made it very clear that they had no plans to release any of the 3,500,000 shares, which could be made available to the public without the passage of this bill.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It is quite obvious the hon. member has spent more time in the pulpit than in business.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: They made it clear also that the principal owners had no plans to dispose of their shares. That was admitted quite frankly.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: What you do not know about business would fill a book.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I am prepared to give the hon. member for Kootenay East an opportunity to take part in this debate if he will rise in his place. I am quite sure the hon. member is not prepared to go back to his constituency and tell the miners in Kootenay East that he was for a project of this sort.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I am all for the passage of this bill. I would not filibuster any bill.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay East is not going to stand up and tell me that this stock-splitting project is not designed exclusively to make fortunes for people who are gambling on the stock market. There has been no suggestion that the operations of this company have been limited in any way because of the fact that this legislation has not been passed.
As a matter of fact the officers of the company indicated that the price of their shares has gone up since the members of this party drew attention to the fact that Trans Mountain has been such a profitable undertaking. The fact that every $10 share that was acquired is now worth about $120 would suggest that those who put their money in it have done very well. The officers also told us that on the basis of their estimates for last year they have nearly $7 million clear after paying corporation taxes.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Is it not true that they are making that money from oil going to the United States?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Again I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Kootenay East delay his remarks at this time and allow me to proceed with my argument.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The hon. member is not making an argument.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: We will see that he is given an opportunity before the legislation passes. The fact that every $10 invested in Trans Mountain is now worth about $120 suggests to the people who are forced to pay these high prices for petroleum products-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The Americans are paying it; what is the hon. member kicking about?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: There cannot be two people speaking at the same time.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: You tried to last night when I was speaking.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I am prepared to see that the hon. member has an opportunity. In the meantime the hon. member for Kootenay East has not risen in the committee and he has not spoken in the house.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I did rise in the committee and I did speak in the committee.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The hon. member did not go on record in the committee as indicating that this was a fine thing for Canada.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Certainly I did.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: These people came to parliament under false pretenses, asking for legislation to be passed with a view to making it possible for more people to participate in the operation of a company like this, when they also made it clear that they had no plans to issue the remaining 3,500,000 shares, which they could do, and that the main owners had no plans for disposing of their shares. We feel that the members of parliament should be concerned about the very high prices people are compelled to pay for their petroleum products as a result of stocksplitting schemes of this sort.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: That is all nonsense.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: This means an increase in value of the shares from $10 to $120 in six years' time, and at the same time imposing an unfair tariff on the people who are buying the products.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The United States consumers.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I suggest to the hon. member for Kootenay East that he take time to read "Oil and Turmoil" by Morden Lazarus, who discusses the oil situation. This interesting book points out that Imperial Oil, which
Private Bills
is one of the companies interested in Trans Mountain is 70 per cent owned by Standard Oil of New Jersey.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: And the provincial government invited them to come into Saskatchewan.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes. We have a perfectly good reason, with the provincial government not being able to compete with Imperial, Gulf and Texaco, these international cartels. I should like to remind my hon. friend that while Canada is dominated by these large oil companies Mexico has been able to take action in the field of oil. In the December, 1956, issue of The Nation there is an interesting article entitled "Oil for Progress". This article reports what Mexico has been able to do in this field. I quote:
In 1937, the price of gasoline in Mexico City was 20 per cent higher than the average price in the United States. Today, the United States price is 80 per cent higher than the Mexican.
It's worth noting that as regards labour conditions in Mexico, the average wage in privately-owned manufacturing industries during 1955 was about $1 a day; in the oil industry it was over $4. This contrasts sharply with pre-expropriation wage scales, when oil workers' salaries were equal to or lower than prevailing inadequate wages. Pemex has a program of workers benefits unique in Mexico. It includes free schooling, free medical care for workers and their families, pensions and a sayings fund. Last year the company spent $5 million on medical care and schooling . . .
The article points out that from 1938 to 1955 Pemex produced 1,005 million barrels, mostly for national consumption, on which taxes were paid amounting to 5 million pesos. Compared with that, from 1900 to 1937 their production was 1,895 million barrels of oil and they paid to the federal treasury only 77 million pesos. If a country like Mexico is able to stand up to those moguls; to introduce public ownership into the field of oil; to have prices which are 80 per cent lower than in the United States, as compared with 20 per cent higher before public ownerships, we should have a look at this proposition which asks that a further toll be levied on the consumers of petroleum products.
We are spending a very sizeable amount of Canadian funds in connection with our responsibilities in the Middle East. Hon. members should not forget that one of the reasons we are involved in the Middle East is as a result of the large investments in oil in that area.
Another book I should like to recommend to the hon. member for Kootenay East is "The Empire of Oil" by Harvey O'Connor.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Who is Harvey O'Connor?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member will find some of his books in the library. He writes a very good treatise on the empire of oil. One of the things he mentions is that Standard of New Jersey was one of the companies that

Private Bills
was mentioned by I. G. Farben as having made it possible for Hitler to gain information without which it would have been impossible to have waged the 1939-45 war.
This is information that was seized by the United States army. Standard of New Jersey was quite prepared to make available to I. G. Farben and Hitler top secret information which, according to Farben, if it had been denied, would have made it impossible for the Germans to carry on the war.
There is an interesting reference to the sheikdom of Kuwait. There has been a great deal of interest recently in the visit to this continent of King Saud. According to Mr. O'Connor the money flooding in upon King Saud, if spread equally among his 6 million subjects, would give them an annual income of only $23 apiece. However, if he were to make available to them his revenues from oil it would give them another-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Is this Karl Marx Jr.?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
No-another $750. In contrast to that, the annual average income was $50 per person.
In view of the fact that these international cartels are forcing the people in various countries to pay these fabulous prices for petroleum products and to build up these incredible fortunes, I think this parliament should not act on the advice of the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) and give its approval to the splitting of these shares to make it possible for those who want to make easy fortunes to get something for nothing, when they are unwilling to do hard work with their hands. They want to share in the fortune which King Saud thinks it is quite all right to have for himself while his subjects live in such depressed conditions.
I hope that now I have concluded my remarks the hon. member for Kootenay East will give his reasons for recommending this measure to parliament.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I thought the member for Kootenay East wanted to speak.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I did not say I wanted to speak. I wanted to vote.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kootenay East, who has had so much to say, is not prepared to get up and say something now.
There is one fact about this bill which I feel the house should know and that is the remarkable disingenuous way, shall I say, in which the members of the committee were treated by the officials of this company. The president of the company was asked at one point of the proceedings what were the

shareholdings of the directors of the company. All he could tell us was that they had the two shares necessary to qualify as directors. It was not until later that we were informed that in April of last year-this has not been mentioned either by the sponsor of this bill or by the company officials before the committee-30,000 shares were set aside at $35 each, when they were selling at $50 on the market, for the officers and directors of the company to take up when they wished to do so.
We were not told that. We were told, in fact, the company had no intention whatever of placing on the market any major holdings that were in the treasury. No mention was made of this step which was taken in April of last year to provide 30,000 shares for the benefit of company officials and directors. They were options to buy, some of which have been taken up.
In addition there is another incident that interests me a great deal. I asked the president of this company this question, which appears on page 43 of the proceedings of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines:
Are these oil companies or what kind of business are they in?
There had been a reference to the companies which were shareholders in Trans Mountain and Mr. McQuarrie who is, I think, the treasurer of the company, told me this:
They are in all sorts of business; some are investment people, insurance companies, and all sorts of people who have money to invest.
Now that, to put it quite bluntly, was simply not true, because all sorts of companies are not in this Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. All the shares held by companies are held by oil companies. There are six of them who are major shareholders. They are: Canadian Gulf Oil Company; Imperial Oil Limited; Shell Oil Company of Canada Limited; Standard Oil Company of B. C. Limited; Union Oil Company of California and Richfield Oil Corporation. These companies between them hold 670,000 shares of this company. Then we have a pipe-line construction company, the Bechtel Company, which holds 130,000 shares.
In addition to that we have 14 other oil companies which among them own 250,000 shares. They are: Anglo-Canadian Oil Company Limited; The Calgary and Edmonton Corporation Limited; Calvan Consolidated Oil and Gas Limited; Central Leduc Oils Limited; Del Rio Producers Limited; Home Oil Company Limited; Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited; National Petroleum Corporation Limited; Pacific Petroleum Limited;

Royalite Oil Company Limited; Security Freehold Petroleums Limited; Selburn Oil Company Limited; Trans Empire Oils Limited and Triad Oil Company Limited.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Are any of those insurance companies?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I cannot see that any are in the insurance business, nor are they in all kinds of business. They are all oil companies. We were told that among the corporation shareholders we would find companies engaged in all sorts of business. I submit to you, sir, that when a company sends officials before a committee of this house and those officials treat the committee in such a cavalier manner, then this house should
Private Bills
be cautious indeed about granting the demands of such a company controlled and operated by such officials. We are still waiting, Mr. Chairman, to find some reasonable proof that the company really wishes to have a wide distribution of its shares. The officials of this company did not tell us these were oil companies.
Progress reported.

ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL MUSEUM, BADDECK, N.S.
speechtext:
1.	What was the final cost of the Alexander Graham Bell museum erected in Baddeck in 1956?
2.	Did the provincial government share in this project?
3.	If so, in what respect and at what cost?
Answer by: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	$409,794.
2.	Yes.
3.	The province of Nova Scotia has shared in this project through its agreement to contribute to the federal government the area of approximately 14 acres of land on which the museum stands. The department has no record of the cost incurred by the government of the province of Nova Scotia in obtaining this land for use by the federal government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMMUNITION WORKERS, RENOUS AND KAMLOOPS   WAGE REPORT
speechtext:
1.	Has the committee which was established to review the arrangements for determining wages for ammunition workers at Renous, New Brunswick, and Kamloops, British Columbia, now finished its work?
2.	If so, has it made a report?
3.	What are the terms of such report?
Answer by: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
1.	Yes.
2.	Yes.
3.	Since the report was prepared by civil servants and is of an advisory nature, its contents are considered privileged. Action which may be taken as a result of the report would be made known in accordance with the customary practice regarding such matters.
